sources.title: Jhoti, Chita, Muruja
sources.author: Government of Odisha web portal; no personal byline
sources.date_limit: Undated content. Dynamic site footer Last Updated23/11/2026 is not a verified article publication or fieldwork date; substantially identical text occurs in indexed Odisha Reference Annual2011.
sources.type: Official cultural overview, not a documented field sample or universal practice survey
sources.access: Original portal opened and read through web tool; direct HTML download also successful. Works-department mirror originally timed out.
precise_locators: Jhoti paragraph1: white rice paste/pithau on mud walls and floors
Jhoti paragraph3: fingers and cloth attached to twig
Jhoti paragraph4: grain bins, threshold, earthen pots and other household surfaces
Muruja paragraphs1–2: coloured powders and their application
supported_claims: The official overview describes Jhoti/Chita using white rice paste, called pithau, on walls and floors.
It also lists grain bins, thresholds and earthen pots as surfaces; an article need not confine the practice to a floor.
It distinguishes powder-based Muruja from the rice-paste practice, a useful material distinction rather than an exhaustive naming taxonomy.
limits: Do not repeat its timeless, pristine, universal women's-practice or every-occasion assertions.
The wrist-sprinkling sentence is garbled in current HTML; omit rather than repair from assumption.
No chemical/pigment recipes, sanitation or safety claims needed.
Do not make the separate tattoo paragraph part of Jhoti technique.
No government photograph/image reuse licence inferred.
family_aliases: Odisha Reference Annual2011 entry: indexed identical prose, not separately inspected or independent corroboration
sources.suggested_final_allocation: 140–160 words including title/dek/footnote and any factual brief repetition

sources.title: Socio-Cultural Context and Aesthetic Values of 'Jhoti'
sources.publisher: Man in Society, Department of Anthropology, Utkal University
sources.type: Authored academic cultural synthesis. Inspected passages do not establish a fieldwork sample or date. Original books cited in its bibliography were not read for this task.
sources.access: Reused actual PDF saved during previous Gouri research; checked source text against current original university URL and personally inspected existing/new page renders.
personally_visually_inspected: PDF119/printed118 designs and unsupported decline assertions
supported_claims: Printed117 describes water added to rice paste for painting, a small cloth held by the middle finger to carry paste and redipped when dry, and an alternative cloth-tipped stick.
Printed118 lists lotus designs with different petal counts; it supports variation in patterns, not one mandatory template.
Printed117 discusses prepared earthen walls/floors and the white mark against that surface; no claim that modern surfaces cannot carry Jhoti is adopted.
sources.claim_locator: Technique paragraph in right column of printed117, beginning after the discussion of rice types; pattern examples in upper-right column of printed118.
limits: Preserve existing Bali Trutiya boat/trade quarantine; do not reuse it as history.
Do not adopt universal caste/religious participation, ancient origin, unchanging sacred rules, nutrition, modern decline or sticker-disapproval assertions.
Do not convert descriptive cow-dung preparation into a sanitation claim or instruction.
No present-day demonstration or personally observed making is claimed.

Government overview and journal agree on basic finger/stick methods, but agreement does not establish independent field observation. Use the paper for its distinct cloth/reservoir detail and bounded attribution.
sources.bibliography_scope: Printed120 cites Dash2015, Padmavati Mohapatra Chita1999, Odisha Cultural Forum1978 and Surendranath Panigrahi2016. These are uninspected references, not additional evidence families.
sources.suggested_final_allocation: 100–140 words including note and any description repeated in the brief; preserve existing stable source ID

sources.title: Raghurajpur women showcase special specimens of everyday art form 'jhoti'
sources.author: Minati Singha
sources.event_date_scope: Report dated21December2023 says Wednesday;20December is a calendar inference, not necessary for the article. Prefer December2023.
sources.type: Original named-reporter account with named participant and organizer testimony
sources.access: Full original article body read through web tool; direct HTML download also successful.
precise_locators: Opening paragraph: Odisha Lalit Kala Akademi and Culture Department competition involving Raghurajpur women
Paragraph beginning Nobody had taught us: Rukmini Mohapatra's quoted learning account
Final paragraphs: prizes and organizer's future plan, not evidence of later events
supported_claims: A December2023 competition in Raghurajpur presented local women's Jhoti work publicly.
Participant Rukmini Mohapatra described learning through mothers, aunts and grandmothers; attribute this account to her, rather than asserting every girl's experience.
The report quotes organizer Sudarshan Pattnaik describing recognition of domestic artistic skill as an aim; this is his stated aim, not measured impact.
limits: No statewide participation rate, current recurring event, livelihood outcome or uninterrupted transmission claimed.
Do not extend a participant's broad quotation to all women or all Odisha households.
Do not reuse TOI's photograph without permission.
No need to quote directly; fresh paraphrase avoids extracting a long interview passage.
sources.suggested_final_allocation: 90–130 words including note and any factual brief repetition

family_independence: Three publication families: official overview, authored2020journal and original2023report. Government mirrors/2011annual are one family; the journal's cited books are not newly verified families. The report's named testimony supplies independently reported contemporary context. Do not present generic shared technique claims as three separate field observations.
